caption:
Diaper rubbing the cord stump? Fold the top of the diaper down, below the stump.

WHY: the stump heals best when it stays clean and dry. With the diaper folded below it, pee can't soak it and the waistband can't rub it (AAP).

HOW (AAP):
1. At every change, fold the front of the diaper down so its top edge sits below the stump.
2. Keep the stump clean and dry, open to the air. There's no need to put alcohol on it.
3. Leave it be. It dries, shrinks and falls off on its own, usually by the time your baby is 3 weeks old.
4. A few drops of blood on the diaper around the time it falls off is normal.

THE CATCH: call your baby's doctor if you see red skin around the base, a yellowish discharge that smells bad, or your baby cries when you touch it. If the cord is actively bleeding, call right away. If it's still there after 3 weeks, book a visit.

Do this: next diaper, fold it below the stump.

Send this to someone with a brand-new baby.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#newborn #newbornbaby #newparents #babycare #umbilicalcord
first_comment: Sources (checked Oct 27 2026): AAP, HealthyChildren.org, 'Umbilical Cord Care in Newborns' (healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/bathing-skin-care/Pages/Umbilical-Cord-Care.aspx, updated 7/6/2025): keep the stump "clean and dry as it shrivels and eventually falls off"; "There is no need to use alcohol on the umbilical cord stump"; "keep the diaper folded below the cord to keep urine from soaking it"; should "fall off by the time your baby is 3 weeks old", otherwise see the doctor; a few drops of blood around the time it falls off "is normal"; "if the cord actively bleeds, call your baby's doctor immediately"; call for foul-smelling yellowish discharge, red skin around the base, or crying when it's touched. Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, 'Umbilical cord care' (library.sheffieldchildrens.nhs.uk/umbilical-cord-care): keep the cord dry and clean; keep it out of the nappy area; "try not to touch the cord"; it usually falls off 5 to 15 days after birth.

caption:
Under 3? Toothpaste is just a smear the size of a grain of rice.

WHY: fluoride toothpaste protects new teeth from decay. A tiny amount gives that protection to a child who can't spit well yet (NHS, AAP).

HOW (NHS, AAP):
1. Start brushing as soon as the first tooth comes through.
2. Under 3: a smear of fluoride toothpaste, about the size of a rice grain. The NHS says use one with at least 1,000 ppm fluoride.
3. From 3 to 6: a pea-sized amount.
4. Brush twice a day, and make one of them last thing before bed.
5. Afterwards, spit the extra out. Don't rinse with water: it washes the fluoride away.

THE CATCH: you put the toothpaste on the brush, not them, and keep the tube out of reach. Most kids need a hand with brushing until about 8 (AAP).

Do this: tonight, a rice-grain smear, then brush.

Send this to whoever does bedtime.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#toddler #toddlerlife #babyteeth #toddlertips #parentingtips
first_comment: Sources (checked Oct 27 2026): NHS Best Start in Life, 'Baby and toddler tooth care' (nhs.uk/best-start-in-life/how-to-take-care-of-your-baby-or-toddlers-teeth/): "Start brushing your child's teeth as soon as the first milk tooth comes through"; "use a smear (the size of a grain of rice) of toothpaste for babies and toddlers up to 3 years"; "use a pea sized amount of toothpaste for children aged 3 to 6"; toothpaste with at least 1,000 ppm fluoride; brush last thing at night and one other time; "do not rinse with water after brushing as it washes away fluoride". AAP, HealthyChildren.org, 'Toothbrushing Tips for Young Children' (healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/oral-health/Pages/Toothbrushing-Tips-for-Young-Children.aspx, updated 5/14/2025): under 3 "a smear of fluoride toothpaste (about the size of a grain of rice)"; ages 3 to 6 "a pea-sized amount"; brush twice a day; spit out and don't rinse right after; children usually need help until 8; an adult places the toothpaste and keeps it out of reach.
